sceneHappening: Women who supported him, the sower, a storm, a man in the tombs, and two daughters
summary: Soon afterward Jesus goes through cities and villages proclaiming the good news of the Kingdom of God, with the twelve and some women who had been healed of evil spirits and sicknesses: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward; Susanna; and many others, who provide for them out of their possessions. A great crowd gathers, and he tells the parable of the sower: seed on the path is trampled and eaten by birds, seed on rock withers for lack of moisture, seed among thorns is choked, and seed on good soil bears a hundredfold. When the disciples ask what it means, he says, "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'" The seed is the word of God, and the soils are four ways of receiving it. He says no one lights a lamp and hides it under a bowl, and "Take heed therefore how you hear." When his mother and brothers can't reach him for the crowd, he says, "My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God, and do it." On the lake one day he says, "Let's go over to the other side." He falls asleep, a windstorm comes down, and the boat is filling. They wake him: "Master, master, we are dying!" He rebukes the wind and the raging water, and there is calm. "Where is your faith?" They are afraid and marvel, "Who then is this, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?" On the other side, in the country of the Gerasenes, a man from the city who has had demons for a long time, who wears no clothes and lives in the tombs, falls at Jesus' feet: "What do I have to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I beg you, don't torment me." "What is your name?" "Legion." They beg not to be sent into the abyss and ask to enter a herd of pigs, and the herd rushes down the cliff into the lake and drowns. The people come out, find the man sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind, and they are afraid and ask Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with him, but Jesus says, "Return to your house, and declare what great things God has done for you." He goes and proclaims throughout the city what Jesus had done for him. Back across the lake, Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, begs Jesus to come for his only daughter, about twelve, who is dying. On the way, a woman who has had a flow of blood for twelve years and could not be healed by anyone touches the fringe of his cloak and is healed at once. "Who touched me?" She comes trembling and tells all. "Daughter, your faith has made you healthy. Go in peace." A messenger arrives: "Your daughter is dead." "Don't be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed." At the house he lets in only Peter, John, James, and the girl's parents. "Don't weep; for she isn't dead, but sleeping." They laugh at him, knowing she is dead. He takes her hand: "Child, arise!" Her spirit returns and she rises at once; he tells them to give her something to eat, and charges them to tell no one what has happened.
whySettingMatters: Luke is the Gospel that most notices women. The women of 8:1-3 are the ones who "provided for them out of their possessions," that is, patrons who financed the mission, and Joanna's husband worked for Herod Antipas, which means one of Jesus' supporters was connected to the court. Mary of Magdala is named here and is not the sinful woman of chapter 7; the idea that she was is a later tradition and not in the text. Luke's version of the sower is shorter than Mark's, and he adds that "those who hear the word" should hold it fast. In the storm scene, Luke says "master" for Jesus where the other Gospels say "teacher." The country of the Gerasenes is debated; manuscripts also read Gadarenes and Gergesenes, and Gerasa lies far from the lake. Luke adds "the abyss," the place of the demons' final confinement, and says the man had no clothes. Pigs were unclean, and the herd points to a largely Gentile area. Unlike in Mark, Jesus here sends the man to tell what God has done and Luke says he told what "Jesus" had done, so for Luke the two are the same. The two women, one twelve years ill and the other twelve years old, are both called "daughter" or "child," and the older one's touch of the fringe is a risk under the purity laws.

questions: Women supported Jesus' mission out of their own resources. What does it mean that Luke puts that in?
Jesus says his true family are those who hear and do the word. What kind of belonging does he offer?
The people of the region ask Jesus to leave, and the healed man wants to go with him. What does Jesus' answer tell each of them?
Jairus is told, "Don't be afraid; only believe." What would believing mean to a father who has just heard his daughter has died?
